answers:
1. It was the pressure data from our existing SCADA sensors, so we didn't buy any new hardware. I don't know how long it had been sitting there before we used it.

2. I can't point to one specific signature in the data, I don't have that detail handy. The one that stands out is a major main leak under an elementary school that our field tech Carlos Ruiz traced using the model's alerts.

3. The drop from 14% to 9% took 18 months. I can't say how much of it came from leaks found this way versus other work, so I'd rather not claim all of it. It saves about 410 million gallons a year.

4. The early alerts were rough, about 30% were false positives in the first months. Honestly, I don't think the machine learning was essential, and simple threshold rules got us most of the gains. So I'd tell people to start simple with the data they already have. The whole project cost $85,000.

5. It's Dr. Naomi Fischer, Senior Water Systems Engineer, Mesa Valley Water Authority. I've got 12 years at the authority and a PhD from Arizona State.

Your answers supplied the missing material, so I built both pieces from them and kept your phrasing where I could. I left out two things you didn't give me: how long the data sat unused, and what a leak looks like in it. The abstract says nothing on either.

<final>
Finding Leaks with Pressure Data We Already Had

Abstract

Mesa Valley Water Authority found leaks using pressure data from its existing SCADA sensors, with no new hardware. Over 18 months, non-revenue water dropped from 14% to 9%, which saves about 410 million gallons a year. We can't say how much of that drop came from leaks found this way and how much from other work.

One find was a major main leak under an elementary school, which field tech Carlos Ruiz traced using the model's alerts. The early alerts were rough: about 30% were false positives in the first months. I also don't think the machine learning was essential. Simple threshold rules got us most of the gains, and the whole project cost $85,000. This talk covers what we did and why I'd tell other utilities to start simple with the data they already have.

Short Bio

Dr. Naomi Fischer is a Senior Water Systems Engineer at Mesa Valley Water Authority, with 12 years at the authority and a PhD from Arizona State.
</final>
